chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa from Ali ibn al-Hakam from Musa ibn Bakr from Zurara from Humran ibn A'yan from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him)

Regarding a man who left a daughter and a mother, the inheritance is four shares because the daughter has three shares and the mother has one-sixth (one share), and two shares remain, so they are more entitled to them than the paternal uncle, the son of the brother, and the agnates, because the daughter and the mother were specified for them, and they were not specified for the others, so they are returned to them according to their shares.
From him, from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Ash'ari, who said:

A dispute arose between two men from my paternal cousins regarding inheritance, so I suggested to them in writing to refer to him for that, so that they might act according to his opinion. So they both wrote to him, 'May we be your ransom, what do you say regarding a woman who left a husband, a daughter, and a sister from her father and mother?'
And I said to him, 'May I be your ransom, if you see fit to answer us with the truth,' so he sent them a letter.

In the name of Allah, the Merciful, the Compassionate. May Allah grant health to us and to you and improve your health. I understood your letter, you mentioned that a woman died and left a husband, a daughter, and a sister from her father and mother. The share for the husband is one-fourth, and what remains is for the daughter.

key_terms.أَسْهُمٍ: Shares (in the context of fractional division)

ai.seo_question: How is the estate divided when a deceased leaves a husband, daughter, and sister?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the Shia jurisprudential principle of *rad* (returning the surplus to the primary heirs) when the fixed shares do not exhaust the estate, ensuring the daughter and mother retain their proportional portions rather than ceding them to agnatic relatives (*asaba*). The second part highlights the scholarly practice of *al-maktub* (epistolary fatwas), where Imam al-Sadiq (AS) provided precise rulings to specific inquiries, reinforcing the authority of the Imams in resolving complex inheritance disputes involving mixed kinship ties.
